implementation_notes: The .NET unit-testing guidance states the pattern directly - arrange your objects, act on an object, assert that something is as expected - and shows the three sections as comments inside the test method. What replaces the classic Testcase Class fixture is the [Fact]/[Theory] attribute plus the test class constructor (or IAsyncLifetime) for shared setup, with a single call in the test body; NUnit and MSTest use [Test]/[SetUp] but keep the same beats, and Assert.* (or a fluent assertion library) supplies the assert vocabulary.
pitfalls: xUnit stops at the first failed assertion, so a test with several post-conditions reports them one run at a time; use Assert.Multiple (NUnit) or the framework's aggregate form when the assert beat really has several facets.
An async act that is not awaited lets the test method complete before the call does, moving the failure to the assert beat or hiding it entirely.
Sample values copied into both the arrange and the assert beat couple the test to the data; the guidance recommends constants or the minimal passing input instead.
